newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees no French threat to its Mideast role.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees no French threat to its Mideast role.

text.p: The United States has greeted French President Jacques Chirac's Middle East tour with a show of polite support, barbed with gentle reminders of its own key role in the peace process.

Whether or not Chirac hopes to supplant the Americans as key peace-maker, Washington can afford a laid-back attitude, confident that Israel will not accept Paris in any serious mediating role, U.S. analysts say.

Chirac's tour of Syria, Israel, Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt this week played well with the Arabs, and even Iran, with his message that Europe could help rectify the imbalance that Arabs perceive in the U.S.-led peace process.
But a series of incidents during the visits did little to endear the French leader to Israel's right-wing Likud government, diplomats said.

These ranged from a dispute over whether French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette could visit a Palestinian office in East Jerusalem -- he eventually did not go to Israel -- to a scene between Chirac and over-zealous Israeli security men.
Throughout, U.S. officials insisted smilingly that they believed Chirac's tour was a good idea, and that any notion of U.S. resentment at French meddling was "created by the press."

"We have a friendship and an alliance with France and ... a very strong friendship with President Chirac," said State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns. "We think he plays a positive role in the Middle East."
He said Secretary of State Warren Christopher had sent de Charette a "positive, supportive, friendly letter" last weekend that expressed "full support" for Chirac's trip.
U.S. analysts said that in view of the Israeli distrust of Chirac because of what they see as French pro-Arab sympathies, there was no cause for Washington to see France as a threatening competitor.
"The French define themselves out of being an honest broker, so there is no point in getting too upset," said Robert Satloff, director of the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.

The situation was slightly different six months ago, when Christopher undertook a shuttle mission to try to end fighting between Israel and pro-Iranian guerrillas in Lebanon, only to find de Charette criss-crossing his path on a similar bid.

While Christopher spoke publicly of "coordination" with de Charette, his aides made clear their exasperation at the French initiative, especially when de Charette attempted to involve Washington's hated foe Iran in a settlement.

This time, U.S. officials have appeared confident that there is no French hope of direct involvement in talks that U.S. envoy Dennis Ross has been mediating between Israel and the Palestinians over the West Bank town of Hebron.
Israeli officials said they saw no role for any outside mediator other than the United States. "So there was a basic tension even before (Chirac) came" to the Middle East, one official said.
U.S. officials have been careful to underline the unique role they see for themselves, saying the Israelis and Palestinians wanted Washington to be their "sole intermediary."
"No one wants a mini-United Nations in those negotiations, but there's more than enough room in the entire Middle East for more than the United States," Burns said.

One of the factors in the U.S. big-heartedness appears to be an attempted lesson in diplomatic manners to Paris, following a heated spat over a trip to Africa earlier this month by Christopher, his first of the Clinton administration.

French Minister for Cooperation Jacques Godfrain commented sarcastically that he was delighted to see Washington's sudden interest in Africa, a traditional French sphere of influence, just weeks before the U.S. presidential election.

U.S. officials expressed outrage for several days over Godfrain's remarks before the two countries agreed to bury the hatchet late last week. The message now seems to be that the United States will not descend to such cheap shots.
